job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
For our explainer ahead of next Thursday's markup, we want to cover the bill's weak spots. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Here's my read of the text as amended. I've grouped the items by section and flagged the ones I'd lead with at the end.

**Section 2 — Definitions**

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — per-vessel threshold invites fleet-splitting.** The 10,000-ton limit is measured "by a single vessel," so an operator can run several vessels each just under the cap, or rotate hulls, and never trigger the prohibition. There is no aggregation across vessels, operators, affiliates, or contract areas.

2. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — the prohibition isn't actually a prohibition.** Anything up to 10,000 tons per vessel per year is lawful, which is enough to permit sustained pilot- and demonstration-scale mining. Expect critics to note the short title oversells the operative text.

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "per year" is undefined.** The bill doesn't say calendar year, fiscal year, rolling 12 months, or year from effective date. An operator could land 9,999 tons in late December and 9,999 more in early January, and the first partial year after the effective date is unaddressed.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "metric tons" of what, measured how?** Polymetallic nodules are roughly a third water by weight, and the bill doesn't say wet or dry, or where and when tonnage is measured (at collection, at the surface, after dewatering, at offload). That's a factual dispute in every enforcement case.

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — "recovery" and "other mineral resources" are undefined.** It's unclear whether "recovery" covers only lifting material to the surface or also seabed disturbance, test collection, or processing, and whether "mineral resources" reaches sulfides and crusts in the subsoil (the text says "from the seabed," not "seabed and subsoil").

6. **Sec. 2(1)(A) — the depth clause is ambiguous.** "At depths greater than 200 meters" could mean water depth or depth below the seafloor; the latter reading would exclude almost everything. "Seabed" is also undefined, so coverage of deep lakes or inland waters is unclear.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — "the Secretary" is never identified.** The only Secretary in the bill is State (Sec. 6), while the registry sits at NOAA (Commerce). Because this determination is an element of a criminal offense, an undefined decision-maker is a serious drafting defect.

8. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — the "comparable risks" standard is open-ended.** There is no process, no notice-and-comment requirement, no publication requirement, no deadline, and no limiting principle; "any activity" could in theory reach trawling or cable-laying. Tying a 10-year felony to an undefined official's unguided judgment invites void-for-vagueness and nondelegation challenges, and the rule of lenity would push courts to read it narrowly.

9. **Sec. 2(1)(B) — timing of determinations vs. conduct.** The text doesn't say whether a determination applies prospectively only. If it can reach past activity, there's a fair-notice problem; if only prospective, companies can operate until the determination lands.

10. **Sec. 2(2) — "U.S. person" is narrow.** It covers only citizens and "corporations organized under the laws of a State." That omits LLCs, partnerships, trusts, lawful permanent residents, non-citizen nationals, and entities organized under federal, D.C., or territorial law ("State" is undefined). More importantly, it omits foreign subsidiaries and affiliates of U.S. companies—the most obvious avoidance route—and says nothing about U.S. ownership or control.

11. **Sec. 2(3) — "covered vessel" doesn't track the prohibition.** The registry applies only to vessels over 5,000 gross tons "equipped for" recovery, but the prohibition applies to anyone, on any platform, who crosses the tonnage threshold. A sub-5,000-ton vessel, a converted drillship, or a non-vessel platform launching seabed collectors could mine at scale without registering or reporting. "Equipped for" is also undefined (installed? capable of being fitted?).

**Section 3 — Prohibition**

12. **Sec. 3(a) — jurisdictional gap for foreign operators in U.S. waters.** "Any person in the United States" likely doesn't reach a foreign company on a foreign-flagged vessel in the U.S. EEZ or on the outer continental shelf, since "in the United States" generally isn't read to include the EEZ absent a definition. The bill would need to define its geographic scope explicitly.

13. **Sec. 3(a) — "engage in" is undefined and there is no secondary liability.** The bill doesn't reach financing, chartering, insuring, sponsoring an ISA contractor, supplying equipment, or managing operations from the U.S., and it has no attempt, conspiracy, or aiding-and-abetting language. A U.S. parent can fund and direct a foreign subsidiary's mining with no exposure.

14. **Sec. 3(a) — no downstream restrictions.** Nothing bars importing, transporting, processing, or selling seabed minerals in the U.S. Minerals recovered by a foreign affiliate can be landed and processed domestically.

15. **Sec. 3(b) — the grandfather clause is keyed to *exploration* licenses, not commercial recovery.** Exploration licenses (NOAA's under DSHMRA) and ISA exploration contracts generally don't authorize commercial mining, so the clause either does nothing or—on a broad reading—lets any holder of a pre-enactment exploration instrument mine commercially forever. "Exploration license" is also undefined, so it's unclear whether ISA "contracts" or foreign-issued permits qualify.

16. **Sec. 3(b) — no limits on the grandfather.** There is no cap on tonnage, area, or duration; nothing addresses renewal, amendment, expansion, or transfer; and "conducted under" doesn't say what happens if activity exceeds the license's scope. The clause also creates a race to obtain licenses before enactment.

17. **Sec. 3(c) — the environmental-assessment exemption is self-declared.** "For the purpose of" is subjective, and there's no tonnage cap, no agency approval, no definition, no data-sharing requirement, and no prohibition on selling recovered material. Commercial recovery relabeled as "assessment" is the most obvious evasion in the bill.

**Section 4 — Registry**

18. **Sec. 4 — no penalty for noncompliance.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of Section 3; failing to register or report carries no consequence under this Act. (18 U.S.C. § 1001 might reach false certifications, but the bill doesn't say so.)

19. **Sec. 4(a) — no deadline or geographic scope.** The bill doesn't say when registration is due (before operations? within X days?) or whether it applies to foreign-flagged vessels, vessels outside U.S. jurisdiction, or only U.S. vessels. "Operator" is undefined.

20. **Sec. 4(b) — self-certified reports with no verification.** NOAA gets no inspection, boarding, audit, subpoena, or rulemaking authority, no required data elements (tonnage, location, depth), and no public-disclosure mandate. The registry is the only mechanism for policing the 10,000-ton threshold and it relies on the honor system.

**Section 5 — Penalties**

21. **Sec. 5(a) conflicts with Sec. 8.** Civil penalties attach to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act doesn't take effect until 180 days later, so no violation can occur in that window. The inconsistency invites arguments either that the penalty is retroactive or that early conduct is unreachable.

22. **Sec. 5(a) — per-day penalties don't fit an annual-threshold offense.** If the violation is exceeding 10,000 tons in a year, it's unclear which "days" the violation "occurs" on: the day the threshold is crossed, every day after, or every day of the year. That ambiguity will determine whether a penalty is $1 million or hundreds of millions.

23. **Sec. 5(a) — no assessment procedure or enforcer.** The bill doesn't say who assesses civil penalties (NOAA administratively? DOJ in court?), what procedures apply, or how penalties are collected; it sets a maximum but no minimum or inflation adjustment. There is also no injunctive relief, no vessel or mineral forfeiture, and no citizen-suit provision.

24. **Sec. 5(b) — severity amplifies the vagueness problem.** A 10-year felony resting on undefined terms ("recovery," "per year," "comparable risks," an unnamed Secretary) makes a constitutional challenge more likely and makes prosecutors less likely to bring cases. There's also no provision for corporate-officer liability.

**Section 6 — International agreement**

25. **Sec. 6 — unenforceable aspiration.** "Seek to negotiate" imposes no obligation to conclude anything; "equivalent" is undefined; and the 18-month clause is ambiguous (negotiate *by* 18 months, or *begin* seeking within 18 months?). No report to Congress is required, and the bill doesn't address the U.S.'s non-party status under UNCLOS or its relationship with the ISA.

**Section 7 — Duration**

26. **Sec. 7(a) and (b) conflict.** Subsection (a) says the prohibition lasts until Congress affirmatively finds mining safe; subsection (b) sunsets the entire Act after 10 years regardless. Both can't be right, and (b) will likely control.

27. **Sec. 7(a) — the NASEM report has no sponsor.** Nothing in the bill commissions, funds, scopes, or sets a deadline for the National Academies report that Congress is supposed to act on. "Serious harm" is undefined.

28. **Sec. 7(a) — the joint-resolution mechanism is surplusage.** A joint resolution requires passage by both houses and presidential signature—i.e., it's a statute—so Congress could repeal or amend the Act that way (or any other way) regardless. The provision creates a false impression of a special off-ramp.

29. **Sec. 7(b) — sunset with no savings clause.** When the Act "cease[s] to have effect," it's unclear what happens to pending enforcement actions, accrued penalties, or the registry. The fixed date also gives companies a known horizon to plan around (position vessels, secure licenses, wait it out).

**Section 8 — Effective date**

30. **Sec. 8 — 180-day grace period.** Mining is lawful for six months after enactment, and the registry and reporting obligations are subject to the same delay, so there's no baseline data from that period. (The grandfather clause is keyed to enactment rather than the effective date, which does at least avoid a license rush in the gap.)

**Omissions across the bill**

31. **No relationship to existing law.** The bill neither amends nor repeals the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act of 1980, under which NOAA can still issue commercial recovery permits, nor addresses OCSLA for the U.S. continental shelf. Two federal regimes would point in opposite directions.

32. **No rulemaking authority, enforcement authority, or appropriations.** No agency is told to write implementing regulations, the Coast Guard isn't given boarding or inspection powers, and there's no funding, so the registry and the Sec. 2(1)(B) determination process may never be operationalized.

33. **No severability clause.** If a court strikes Sec. 2(1)(B) or the penalty provisions for vagueness, there's no instruction to preserve the rest of the Act.

**If you need to prioritize:** the items most likely to matter in practice are the per-vessel threshold (1), the narrow U.S.-person definition and absence of affiliate/secondary liability (10, 13), the self-declared environmental-assessment exemption (17), the exploration-license grandfather (15–16), the undefined "Secretary" with criminal consequences (7–8), the Sec. 5/Sec. 8 timing conflict (21), and the Sec. 7 internal contradiction (26). Those are the ones a markup amendment would most plausibly target, and the ones opponents would cite first.
